## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Robotics
  Official title       Robotics
  Instructors          J. CARPENTIER, S. BONNABEL, P.B. WIEBER, A. SATHYA (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 28 h (lectures 19 h, tutorials 9 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Modelling]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Machine Learning
  Language             not displayed on the official pages (the master-mva.com description is written in English)
  Assessment           weekly homework (20 %) + project or an article study (80 %); the final exam is a 4 h student seminar of project and report presentations (master-mva.com); non-integral continuous assessment, “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale” (Université Paris-Saclay course detail)
  Prerequisites        undergraduate-level linear algebra; labs (TP) in Python, with basic knowledge of the language and of general programming concepts (functions, loops, recursion, data structures); taking the “Convex optimization” course by A. d’Aspremont at the same time is recommended (master-mva.com)
  -------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with an M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics who has never modelled a robot, and who wants to understand how modelling, planning, control, estimation and learning fit together on a machine that moves in the physical world.

**Empirical first**: integrate the frictionless oscillator $\ddot x = -x$ with the explicit Euler scheme and a step of 0.1 s, and after 1,000 steps its energy has been multiplied by about 21,000; the semi-implicit scheme, one line different, keeps it within 5 % ([ch. 0](#ch0)). A humanoid whose centre of mass is 0.8 m high and which is pushed at 0.5 m/s must put its foot about 14 cm ahead, within a few tenths of a second, or fall ([ch. 7](#ch7)).

Both facts are about dynamics, and dynamics is the thread of the course. A robot is a mechanical system whose state obeys Newton's laws, whose sensors are noisy, and whose motions must avoid obstacles and respect contact. Each chapter turns one of these constraints into a mathematical problem — a least-squares problem, a graph search, an optimal control problem, a filtering problem, a stochastic optimisation — and into an algorithm that runs on a real robot.

The course leans on [Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html), which the official page recommends taking at the same time. Its estimation chapter meets [3D Computer Vision](../s1-3d-computer-vision/index.html) and [Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html); its learning chapter opens the door to [Reinforcement Learning](../s2-reinforcement-learning/index.html) in semester 2.

### What you will be able to do

-   Model a robot as a kinematic tree: compute its forward kinematics, its Jacobians and its Lagrangian dynamics, and simulate it with an integrator suited to mechanics.
-   Plan collision-free paths with A\*, probabilistic roadmaps and rapidly-exploring random trees, and bound the failure probability of a sampling-based planner.
-   Solve inverse kinematics by damped least squares, exploit redundancy with null-space projections, and write whole-body control as a quadratic program.
-   Design computed-torque and PD-plus-gravity controllers and prove their stability with a Lyapunov function.
-   Derive the linear-quadratic regulator from dynamic programming, apply Pontryagin's principle, and optimise trajectories with iLQR and model predictive control.
-   Estimate the state of a robot with Kalman, extended and invariant Kalman filters, and register two point clouds.
-   Train a policy by policy gradient, relate it to optimal control, and quantify the simulation-to-reality gap.
-   Generate a walking pattern with the linear inverted pendulum, the zero-moment point and the capture point.
-   Build a safety filter with a control barrier function, and argue about the responsibilities of robotics research.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com observes that a large part of the recent progress in robotics has come with advances in machine learning, optimisation and computer vision. The course introduces the general conceptual tools behind these advances, and shows how they let robots perceive the world and perform tasks that go beyond factory automation, from highly dynamic somersaults to mountain hikes.

It covers modelling and simulation of robotic systems, motion planning, inverse problems for motion control, optimal control and reinforcement learning. It includes practical exercises with state-of-the-art robotics libraries, and a broader reflection on our responsibilities when doing research and innovation in robotics.

master-mva.com organises the course in 8 sessions of 3 h and a 4 h final exam held as a student seminar, and lists seven themes. ### Course outline

-   **Review: least squares, rotations, integration and Gaussian conditioning** — the pseudo-inverse and its damped version, equality-constrained quadratic programs, Rodrigues' formula, explicit and semi-implicit Euler, Gaussian conditioning.
-   **Modelling and simulation of robotic systems** — configuration spaces, rigid motions, product of exponentials, Jacobians and statics, Lagrangian dynamics and its skew-symmetry, rigid-body algorithms and libraries, contact and time stepping.
-   **Motion planning** — the configuration-space formulation, A\* and its optimality, probabilistic roadmaps with a completeness bound, RRT and RRT\*, from paths to trajectories.
-   **Inverse problems for robot control** — inverse geometry by Levenberg–Marquardt, differential inverse kinematics and redundancy, computed torque, PD plus gravity compensation, task-space quadratic programs.
-   **Optimal control and trajectory optimisation** — Bellman's principle, the LQR, Pontryagin's principle, direct transcription, iLQR and DDP, model predictive control and its stability.
-   **Perception and estimation** — Bayes and Kalman filters, the EKF and observability, invariant errors on Lie groups, batch estimation and SLAM, cameras and point-cloud registration.
-   **Reinforcement learning for robotics** — MDPs and their link with optimal control, the policy-gradient theorem, PPO and SAC, the simulation lemma and sim-to-real transfer, imitation learning.
-   **Legged locomotion** — centroidal dynamics, the zero-moment point and the support polygon, the linear inverted pendulum, the capture point, MPC walking pattern generation, whole-body control.
-   **Responsible robotics** — safety standards and control barrier functions, research integrity and statistics of robot trials, a responsible-innovation framework, dual use, environment and work.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — differentiable contact simulation, whole-body MPC, learned locomotion and manipulation, Lie-group estimation, certified learning (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before session 1. Proposition 0.3 (damped least squares), Proposition 0.4 (KKT systems) and Proposition 0.9 (Gaussian conditioning) come back in ch. 3, 4 and 5 without warning.
-   After each session, do the exercises of the *Practice* column; the official weekly homework counts for 20 % of the grade, and the homework suggested in the plan has the right size.
-   Rerun each code block and change one parameter at a time: the step of the integrator, the damping of the inverse kinematics, the horizon of the MPC, the exploration noise of the policy.
-   Choose the project or the article study early (session 4 at the latest): it counts for 80 % and is presented at the final seminar.
-   Python environment: NumPy and SciPy suffice for every block; all data are synthetic, with fixed seeds. For the projects, the open-source libraries Pinocchio, MuJoCo and Crocoddyl are the natural next step.

## 0. Review: least squares, rotations, integration and Gaussian conditioning {#ch0}

Four M1 tools carry most of the course. Least squares solves inverse kinematics and estimation problems; quadratic programs with equality constraints encode control; rotations describe every rigid body; numerical integration turns equations of motion into simulations.

This chapter states each tool in the form used later, with short proofs. The last section recalls Gaussian conditioning, on which the Kalman filter of [ch. 5](#ch5) rests.

### Least squares and the pseudo-inverse

Robotics constantly solves linear systems that have too many or too few equations. A task in the plane constrains two coordinates of a seven-joint arm; twenty camera measurements constrain six pose parameters. The pseudo-inverse handles both cases at once.

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse]{.tag} Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ have the singular value decomposition $A = U \Sigma V^\top$, with singular values $\sigma_1 \geq \dots \geq \sigma_r > 0$. Its pseudo-inverse is
$$
A^+ = V \Sigma^+ U^\top,
$$
where $\Sigma^+ \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$ has $1/\sigma_i$ in position $(i, i)$ for $i \leq r$ and zeros elsewhere.

When $A$ has full row rank, $A^+ = A^\top (A A^\top)^{-1}$; when it has full column rank, $A^+ = (A^\top A)^{-1} A^\top$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.2 — Minimum-norm least squares]{.tag} For every $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$, the vector $x^\star = A^+ b$ minimises $\|A x - b\|$, and among all minimisers it has the smallest norm.

::: proof
Write $y = V^\top x$ and $c = U^\top b$. Orthogonal matrices preserve norms, so
$$
\|A x - b\|^2 = \sum_{i \leq r} (\sigma_i y_i - c_i)^2 + \sum_{i > r} c_i^2 .
$$

The second sum does not depend on $x$. The first one vanishes exactly when $y_i = c_i / \sigma_i$ for $i \leq r$; the coordinates $y_i$ with $i > r$ are free.

Since $\|x\| = \|y\|$, the minimiser of smallest norm sets the free coordinates to zero. That vector is $y = \Sigma^+ c$, that is $x = V \Sigma^+ U^\top b = A^+ b$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Near a rank drop, some $\sigma_i$ is tiny and $c_i / \sigma_i$ explodes. For a robot this means huge joint velocities near a singular configuration ([ch. 3](#ch3)). The cure is to penalise the norm of the solution.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — Damped least squares]{.tag} For $\lambda > 0$, the unique minimiser of $\|A x - b\|^2 + \lambda \|x\|^2$ is
$$
x_\lambda = (A^\top A + \lambda I)^{-1} A^\top b = A^\top (A A^\top + \lambda I)^{-1} b .
$$

In the coordinates of Theorem 0.2, $y_i = \sigma_i c_i / (\sigma_i^2 + \lambda)$, so that every coordinate is bounded by $|c_i| / (2 \sqrt{\lambda})$.

::: proof
The objective is strongly convex; setting its gradient to zero gives the normal equations $(A^\top A + \lambda I) x = A^\top b$.

The second expression follows from the identity $(A^\top A + \lambda I) A^\top = A^\top (A A^\top + \lambda I)$, multiplied on the left and on the right by the two inverses.

The diagonal form follows by substituting the SVD. Finally $\sigma^2 + \lambda \geq 2 \sigma \sqrt{\lambda}$, by the inequality between arithmetic and geometric means, which gives the bound. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The second form is the one used in practice: it inverts an $m \times m$ matrix, and $m$ (the task dimension) is usually smaller than $n$ (the number of joints).

### Quadratic programs with equality constraints

Whole-body control ([ch. 3](#ch3)), the LQR ([ch. 4](#ch4)) and walking pattern generation ([ch. 7](#ch7)) all reduce to minimising a convex quadratic under linear constraints.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — KKT system]{.tag} Let $H \succ 0$ and let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times n}$ have full row rank. The problem
$$
\min_x \ \tfrac12 x^\top H x + g^\top x \quad \text{subject to} \quad A x = b
$$
has a unique solution $x^\star$. With a multiplier $\nu^\star$, it is the unique solution of the linear system
$$
\begin{pmatrix} H & A^\top \\ A & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} x^\star \\ \nu^\star \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} -g \\ b \end{pmatrix}.
$$

::: proof
The feasible set is an affine subspace, non-empty because $A$ is onto, and the objective is strongly convex on it: the minimiser exists and is unique.

At the minimiser, the gradient $H x^\star + g$ is orthogonal to $\ker A$, hence lies in the range of $A^\top$: this is the first block row. The second block row is feasibility.

The matrix is invertible. If $H x + A^\top \nu = 0$ and $A x = 0$, then $x^\top H x = -x^\top A^\top \nu = 0$, so $x = 0$; then $A^\top \nu = 0$ and $\nu = 0$ by the rank assumption. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Inequality constraints (torque limits, friction cones, obstacle half-planes) require active-set or interior-point solvers; they are the subject of the [Convex Optimization](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html) course and of chapter 16 of Nocedal and Wright's textbook.

### Rotations and the exponential map

::: def
[Definition 0.5 — The rotation group]{.tag} The special orthogonal group is
$$
SO(3) = \{ R \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} : R^\top R = I, \ \det R = 1 \}.
$$
For $\omega \in \mathbb{R}^3$, the *hat* map gives the skew-symmetric matrix $[\omega]_\times$ such that $[\omega]_\times v = \omega \times v$ for every $v$.

Differentiating $R^\top R = I$ shows that $R^\top \dot R$ is skew-symmetric. Hence every motion of a rotation obeys
$$
\dot R = R\, [\omega]_\times ,
$$
where $\omega$ is the angular velocity expressed in the moving (body) frame.
:::

With $\omega$ constant, the solution starting at $I$ is the matrix exponential of $t\, [\omega]_\times$. For skew-symmetric matrices, the exponential has a closed form.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.6 — Rodrigues' formula]{.tag} For a unit vector $u$ and an angle $\theta$,
$$
\exp(\theta [u]_\times) = I + \sin\theta \, [u]_\times + (1 - \cos\theta) \, [u]_\times^2 .
$$
This is the rotation of angle $\theta$ about the axis $u$.

::: proof
For a unit $u$, one checks that $[u]_\times^3 = -[u]_\times$; hence $[u]_\times^{2k+1} = (-1)^k [u]_\times$ and $[u]_\times^{2k+2} = (-1)^k [u]_\times^2$ for $k \geq 0$.

Splitting the exponential series into odd and even powers gives
$$
I + \Big(\sum_{k \geq 0} \tfrac{(-1)^k \theta^{2k+1}}{(2k+1)!}\Big) [u]_\times + \Big(\sum_{k \geq 0} \tfrac{(-1)^k \theta^{2k+2}}{(2k+2)!}\Big) [u]_\times^2 ,
$$
and the two series are $\sin\theta$ and $1 - \cos\theta$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 0.7 — A quarter turn]{.tag} Take $u = e_z$ and $\theta = \pi/2$. Then $\sin\theta = 1$, $1 - \cos\theta = 1$, and $[e_z]_\times^2 = \mathrm{diag}(-1, -1, 0)$.

Rodrigues' formula gives
$$
R = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix},
$$
which sends $e_x$ to $e_y$, as a quarter turn about $z$ should.
:::

### Integrating equations of motion

A simulator advances the state $(x, v)$ of a mechanical system with a fixed step $h$. Two first-order schemes look almost identical:

-   **explicit Euler**: $x_{k+1} = x_k + h v_k$ and $v_{k+1} = v_k + h a(x_k)$;
-   **semi-implicit (symplectic) Euler**: first $v_{k+1} = v_k + h a(x_k)$, then $x_{k+1} = x_k + h v_{k+1}$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.8 — Energy behaviour on the oscillator]{.tag} Apply both schemes to $\ddot x = -x$, whose energy $\tfrac12 (x^2 + v^2)$ is constant.

-   Explicit Euler multiplies the energy by exactly $1 + h^2$ at every step.
-   Semi-implicit Euler conserves exactly the modified energy $x^2 + v^2 - h\, x v$, which differs from twice the energy by at most a factor $1 \pm h/2$.

::: proof
For explicit Euler, the cross terms cancel in
$$
x_{k+1}^2 + v_{k+1}^2 = (x_k + h v_k)^2 + (v_k - h x_k)^2 = (1 + h^2)(x_k^2 + v_k^2).
$$

For the semi-implicit scheme, substitute $v_{k+1} = v_k - h x_k$ and $x_{k+1} = x_k + h v_{k+1}$ into the modified energy and expand; all terms in $h$ and $h^2$ cancel. The comparison follows from $|x v| \leq \tfrac12 (x^2 + v^2)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

With $h = 0.1$ and 1,000 steps, the first factor is $1.01^{1000} \approx 2.1 \times 10^4$. This is the explosion announced in the introduction; the code below confirms both claims and checks Rodrigues' formula against a general-purpose matrix exponential.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import expm

def hat(w):
    """Skew-symmetric matrix [w]x, so that hat(w) @ v == np.cross(w, v)."""
    return np.array([[0, -w[2], w[1]], [w[2], 0, -w[0]], [-w[1], w[0], 0]])

def rodrigues(w):
    th = np.linalg.norm(w)
    if th < 1e-12:
        return np.eye(3) + hat(w)
    K = hat(w / th)
    return np.eye(3) + np.sin(th) * K + (1 - np.cos(th)) * K @ K

w = np.array([0.3, -0.5, 0.8])
R = rodrigues(w)
print("max |Rodrigues - expm| =", np.abs(R - expm(hat(w))).max())
print("R^T R = I:", np.allclose(R.T @ R, np.eye(3)), "| det R =", round(np.linalg.det(R), 12))

# Explicit vs semi-implicit Euler on x'' = -x, step h = 0.1, 1000 steps
h, n = 0.1, 1000
for scheme in ["explicit", "semi-implicit"]:
    x, v = 1.0, 0.0
    for _ in range(n):
        if scheme == "explicit":
            x, v = x + h * v, v - h * x
        else:
            v = v - h * x
            x = x + h * v
    print(f"{scheme:>13} Euler: energy after {n} steps = {0.5 * (x**2 + v**2):.4f} (initial 0.5)")
```

The output gives an energy of about 10,480 for explicit Euler and 0.52 for semi-implicit Euler. Physics engines therefore use semi-implicit schemes, which also extend naturally to contact ([ch. 1](#ch1)).

### Gaussian conditioning

::: prop
[Proposition 0.9 — Conditioning a Gaussian vector]{.tag} Let $(X, Y)$ be a Gaussian vector with means $\mu_X, \mu_Y$ and covariance blocks $\Sigma_{XX}, \Sigma_{XY}, \Sigma_{YY}$, with $\Sigma_{YY} \succ 0$. Given $Y = y$, the vector $X$ is Gaussian, with
$$
\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y] = \mu_X + \Sigma_{XY} \Sigma_{YY}^{-1} (y - \mu_Y),
\qquad
\mathrm{Cov}(X \mid Y) = \Sigma_{XX} - \Sigma_{XY} \Sigma_{YY}^{-1} \Sigma_{YX}.
$$

*Proof sketch.* The vector $X - \Sigma_{XY} \Sigma_{YY}^{-1} Y$ is uncorrelated with $Y$, hence independent of $Y$ since the pair is Gaussian. Writing $X$ as this vector plus a function of $Y$ gives both formulas; see the [Probability and Statistics refresher](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html).
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   The pseudo-inverse gives the minimum-norm least-squares solution; damping bounds it near singularities at the price of a small bias.
-   A strictly convex quadratic under linear equality constraints is solved by one symmetric linear (KKT) system.
-   Rotations form the group $SO(3)$; Rodrigues' formula is the closed form of its exponential map.
-   For mechanics, prefer semi-implicit Euler to explicit Euler: same cost, bounded energy error.
-   Gaussian conditioning is the algebra behind every Kalman filter.
:::

## 1. Modelling and simulation of robotic systems {#ch1}

Before planning or controlling a robot, one needs its model: which configurations it can take, where its end effector is for a given configuration, and how torques produce accelerations. This chapter builds that model, from geometry to dynamics, and ends with simulation and contact.

### Configuration space and rigid motions

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Configuration space, degrees of freedom]{.tag} The *configuration* of a robot is a minimal set of parameters that fixes the position of all its points; the set $\mathcal{Q}$ of configurations is the configuration space, and its dimension is the number of degrees of freedom.

-   A revolute joint contributes an angle (a circle), a prismatic joint a length (an interval of the line).
-   A serial arm with $n$ revolute joints has $\mathcal{Q} = (S^1)^n$, a torus of dimension $n$.
-   A legged robot also has a *floating base*, whose pose lies in $SE(3)$ (below). A quadruped with 12 joints has $6 + 12 = 18$ degrees of freedom, of which only 12 are actuated.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Rigid motions]{.tag} The pose of a frame attached to a rigid body is a rotation $R \in SO(3)$ and a position $p \in \mathbb{R}^3$, stored in a homogeneous matrix
$$
g = \begin{pmatrix} R & p \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in SE(3),
\qquad
g^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} R^\top & -R^\top p \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

Composition of poses is the matrix product: if $g_{ab}$ is the pose of frame $b$ in frame $a$, then $g_{ac} = g_{ab}\, g_{bc}$.
:::

Like $SO(3)$, the group $SE(3)$ has an exponential map. A *twist* $\xi = (v, \omega)$ describes an infinitesimal screw motion; for a revolute joint of unit axis $\omega$ through the point $r$, the twist is $\xi = (-\omega \times r, \omega)$.

### Forward kinematics

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.3 — Product of exponentials]{.tag} Let $\xi_1, \dots, \xi_n$ be the twists of the joints of a serial chain, expressed in the base frame at the reference configuration $q = 0$, and let $g(0)$ be the pose of the end effector there. For every configuration $q$,
$$
g(q) = e^{\hat\xi_1 q_1}\, e^{\hat\xi_2 q_2} \cdots e^{\hat\xi_n q_n}\; g(0).
$$

::: proof
Move the joints one at a time, starting from the last. Rotating joint $n$ by $q_n$, all other joints at zero, moves the end effector rigidly about the fixed axis $\xi_n$: the pose becomes $e^{\hat\xi_n q_n} g(0)$.

Then rotate joint $n-1$. It moves rigidly everything beyond it, including the current axis of joint $n$, about the axis $\xi_{n-1}$, which is still at its reference place because the joints before it have not moved. The pose becomes $e^{\hat\xi_{n-1} q_{n-1}} e^{\hat\xi_n q_n} g(0)$.

Induction down to joint 1 gives the formula. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The formula, due to Brockett, needs no frame per link; Murray, Li and Sastry (chapter 3) build their whole treatment of manipulators on it. For planar arms, elementary trigonometry gives the same result.

::: ex
[Example 1.4 — The planar two-link arm]{.tag} Links of lengths $l_1, l_2$, joint angles $q_1$ (from the horizontal axis) and $q_2$ (relative). The end effector is at
$$
x = l_1 \cos q_1 + l_2 \cos(q_1 + q_2), \qquad y = l_1 \sin q_1 + l_2 \sin(q_1 + q_2).
$$

With $l_1 = 1$ m, $l_2 = 0.8$ m and $q = (0.4, 1.1)$ rad:
$$
(x, y) = (0.978, \ 1.187) \ \text{m}.
$$
:::

### Jacobians, singularities and statics

::: def
[Definition 1.5 — Kinematic Jacobian]{.tag} If $p = f(q)$ is the position of the end effector, its velocity is
$$
\dot p = J(q)\, \dot q, \qquad J(q) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial q}(q).
$$

A configuration where $J$ loses rank is *singular*: some directions of motion of the end effector cannot be produced, and the inverse problems of [ch. 3](#ch3) become ill-conditioned there.
:::

For the arm of Example 1.4, a direct computation gives
$$
\det J(q) = l_1 l_2 \sin q_2 .
$$
The arm is singular when it is fully stretched ($q_2 = 0$) or fully folded ($q_2 = \pi$). At $q = (0.4, 1.1)$ the determinant is $0.713$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.6 — Statics duality]{.tag} To exert a force $f$ on the environment with its end effector, in static equilibrium and without friction in the joints, the robot must apply the joint torques
$$
\tau = J(q)^\top f .
$$

::: proof
By the principle of virtual work, the work of the joint torques in a virtual displacement $\delta q$ equals the work of the force in the induced displacement $\delta p = J \delta q$. Hence $\tau^\top \delta q = f^\top J \delta q$ for every $\delta q$, which gives $\tau = J^\top f$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The same transpose appears in dynamics: contact forces enter the equations of motion through $J_c^\top \lambda$, where $J_c$ is the Jacobian of the contact point.

### Lagrangian dynamics

Let $T(q, \dot q) = \tfrac12 \dot q^\top M(q) \dot q$ be the kinetic energy of the robot and $V(q)$ its potential energy. The matrix $M(q)$ is the *mass matrix*. For a robot made of point masses $m_i$ located at $p_i = f_i(q)$, it is
$$
M(q) = \sum_i m_i\, J_i(q)^\top J_i(q),
$$
since the kinetic energy is $\sum_i \tfrac12 m_i \|J_i \dot q\|^2$. Rigid links add the rotational terms $J_{\omega,i}^\top I_i J_{\omega,i}$ in the same way.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.7 — Equations of motion]{.tag} The Euler–Lagrange equations of the robot read
$$
M(q)\, \ddot q + C(q, \dot q)\, \dot q + g(q) = \tau + J_c(q)^\top \lambda ,
$$
where $g = \nabla V$, $\tau$ are the joint torques, $\lambda$ the contact forces, and
$$
C_{ij} = \sum_k \Gamma_{ijk}\, \dot q_k, \qquad \Gamma_{ijk} = \tfrac12 \Big( \frac{\partial M_{ij}}{\partial q_k} + \frac{\partial M_{ik}}{\partial q_j} - \frac{\partial M_{jk}}{\partial q_i} \Big).
$$

*Proof sketch.* Apply the Euler–Lagrange equations with $L = T - V$:
$$
\frac{d}{dt} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q} = \tau + J_c^\top \lambda .
$$
The first term gives $M \ddot q + \dot M \dot q$. Subtracting $\tfrac12 \dot q^\top (\partial_{q_i} M) \dot q$ and symmetrising the sum over $j, k$ gives the Christoffel symbols $\Gamma_{ijk}$. The generalised forces of the contacts follow from Proposition 1.6.
::::

::: key
[Key result — the equation of every robot]{.tag}
$$
M(q)\, \ddot q + C(q, \dot q)\, \dot q + g(q) = \tau + J_c(q)^\top \lambda
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.8 — Skew-symmetry and energy balance]{.tag} With the Christoffel choice of $C$, the matrix $\dot M - 2C$ is skew-symmetric. Consequently, without contact, the total energy $E = T + V$ obeys
$$
\dot E = \dot q^\top \tau .
$$

::: proof
Since $\dot M_{ij} = \sum_k (\partial_{q_k} M_{ij})\, \dot q_k$, the definition of $\Gamma$ gives
$$
(\dot M - 2C)_{ij} = \sum_k \Big( \frac{\partial M_{jk}}{\partial q_i} - \frac{\partial M_{ik}}{\partial q_j} \Big) \dot q_k ,
$$
which changes sign when $i$ and $j$ are exchanged.

For the energy,
$$
\dot E = \dot q^\top M \ddot q + \tfrac12 \dot q^\top \dot M \dot q + \dot q^\top g .
$$
Substituting $M \ddot q = \tau - C \dot q - g$ leaves $\dot q^\top \tau + \tfrac12 \dot q^\top (\dot M - 2C) \dot q$, and the last term vanishes by skew-symmetry. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Proposition 1.8 says that the joints inject exactly the power $\dot q^\top \tau$. It is the key step of the stability proofs of [ch. 3](#ch3), and a sharp test for a simulator: with $\tau = 0$ the energy must stay constant.

### Rigid-body algorithms and libraries

Forming $M(q)$ and $C(q, \dot q)$ symbolically is hopeless beyond a few joints. Three recursive algorithms over the kinematic tree, collected in Featherstone's monograph, do the work instead:

-   the **recursive Newton–Euler algorithm** computes the inverse dynamics $\tau = \mathrm{ID}(q, \dot q, \ddot q)$ in $O(n)$ operations — a forward pass for velocities and accelerations, a backward pass for forces;
-   the **composite rigid-body algorithm** computes $M(q)$ in $O(n^2)$;
-   the **articulated-body algorithm** computes the forward dynamics $\ddot q$ in $O(n)$, without forming or inverting $M$.

The open-source library Pinocchio (Carpentier and coauthors, 2019) implements these algorithms together with their analytical derivatives, which [ch. 4](#ch4) needs for trajectory optimisation. The MuJoCo simulator (Todorov, Erez and Tassa, 2012) adds contact. Both have Python bindings and are the natural tools for the projects.

### Contact and simulation

Walking and grasping are made of contacts that open and close. A contact is *unilateral*: the bodies cannot interpenetrate, and the ground can push but not pull.

::: def
[Definition 1.9 — Unilateral contact with Coulomb friction]{.tag} Let $\phi(q)$ be the signed distance between two bodies and $\lambda = (\lambda_n, \lambda_t)$ the normal and tangential contact forces. The contact is described by the complementarity condition
$$
0 \leq \phi(q) \ \perp \ \lambda_n \geq 0 ,
$$
meaning that both are non-negative and at least one is zero. Coulomb's law adds the friction cone
$$
\|\lambda_t\| \leq \mu\, \lambda_n ,
$$
with sliding opposed to the tangential force when the bound is reached.
:::

The conditions are non-smooth: velocities jump at impacts. *Time-stepping* schemes (Stewart and Trinkle, 1996) therefore work with impulses over one step. At each step they solve a complementarity problem for the contact impulses, then update the velocities and the positions in the semi-implicit order of [ch. 0](#ch0). MuJoCo relaxes this problem into a convex one, which makes it fast and always solvable, at the price of small artificial penetrations.

Without contact, any good integrator works. The code below takes the two-link arm of Example 1.4 with point masses at the elbow and at the tip, and checks the Jacobian against finite differences. It builds $M(q) = \sum_i m_i J_i^\top J_i$, lets the arm fall freely for 5 s, and monitors the energy (Proposition 1.8).

```python
import numpy as np

l1, l2, m1, m2, g = 1.0, 0.8, 1.0, 0.5, 9.81   # lengths (m), point masses (kg)

def fk(q):
    """Position of the end effector (angles measured from the x axis)."""
    return np.array([l1 * np.cos(q[0]) + l2 * np.cos(q[0] + q[1]),
                     l1 * np.sin(q[0]) + l2 * np.sin(q[0] + q[1])])

def jacobian(q):
    s1, c1 = np.sin(q[0]), np.cos(q[0])
    s12, c12 = np.sin(q[0] + q[1]), np.cos(q[0] + q[1])
    return np.array([[-l1 * s1 - l2 * s12, -l2 * s12],
                     [ l1 * c1 + l2 * c12,  l2 * c12]])

q = np.array([0.4, 1.1])
eps = 1e-6
J_fd = np.column_stack([(fk(q + eps * e) - fk(q - eps * e)) / (2 * eps) for e in np.eye(2)])
print("max |J - J_fd| =", f"{np.abs(jacobian(q) - J_fd).max():.1e}",
      "| det J =", round(np.linalg.det(jacobian(q)), 6), "| l1 l2 sin q2 =", round(l1 * l2 * np.sin(q[1]), 6))

def mass_matrix(q):
    J1 = np.array([[-l1 * np.sin(q[0]), 0.0], [l1 * np.cos(q[0]), 0.0]])  # elbow mass
    return m1 * J1.T @ J1 + m2 * jacobian(q).T @ jacobian(q)            # M = sum m_i J_i^T J_i

def bias(q, dq):
    """Coriolis, centrifugal and gravity terms h(q, dq)."""
    k = m2 * l1 * l2 * np.sin(q[1])
    cor = np.array([-k * (2 * dq[0] * dq[1] + dq[1] ** 2), k * dq[0] ** 2])
    grav = np.array([(m1 + m2) * g * l1 * np.cos(q[0]) + m2 * g * l2 * np.cos(q[0] + q[1]),
                     m2 * g * l2 * np.cos(q[0] + q[1])])
    return cor + grav

def energy(q, dq):
    return 0.5 * dq @ mass_matrix(q) @ dq + m1 * g * l1 * np.sin(q[0]) + m2 * g * fk(q)[1]

# Passive motion (tau = 0) during 5 s: semi-implicit Euler vs Runge-Kutta 4
def rhs(s):
    return np.concatenate([s[2:], np.linalg.solve(mass_matrix(s[:2]), -bias(s[:2], s[2:]))])

s0 = np.array([0.4, 1.1, 0.0, 0.0])
E0 = energy(s0[:2], s0[2:])
for h in [1e-3, 1e-4]:
    s, dev = s0.copy(), 0.0
    for _ in range(round(5 / h)):
        s[2:] += h * rhs(s)[2:]          # velocity first ...
        s[:2] += h * s[2:]               # ... then position with the new velocity
        dev = max(dev, abs(energy(s[:2], s[2:]) - E0) / E0)
    print(f"semi-implicit Euler, h = {h:g} s: max relative energy error {dev:.1e}")
s, h = s0.copy(), 1e-3
for _ in range(5000):
    k1 = rhs(s); k2 = rhs(s + h / 2 * k1); k3 = rhs(s + h / 2 * k2); k4 = rhs(s + h * k3)
    s = s + h / 6 * (k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4)
print(f"Runge-Kutta 4,       h = 0.001 s: relative energy error {abs(energy(s[:2], s[2:]) - E0) / E0:.1e}")
```

The finite differences agree with the analytic Jacobian to about $10^{-10}$. The semi-implicit scheme keeps the energy within 3.6 % at $h = 1$ ms and within 0.35 % at $h = 0.1$ ms: the error is of first order, but bounded.

Runge–Kutta 4 conserves the energy to $2 \times 10^{-10}$, which confirms that the Coriolis terms are right. Yet contact simulators keep first-order schemes, because high-order schemes lose their accuracy at every impact.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   A robot lives in a configuration space; a floating base adds six unactuated degrees of freedom.
-   Forward kinematics is a product of exponentials of joint twists; its Jacobian maps joint velocities to end-effector velocities, and its transpose maps forces to torques.
-   The dynamics always has the form $M \ddot q + C \dot q + g = \tau + J_c^\top \lambda$, with $M \succ 0$ and $\dot M - 2C$ skew-symmetric.
-   Recursive algorithms compute dynamics in linear time; Pinocchio and MuJoCo implement them.
-   Contact is a complementarity condition with a friction cone; simulators handle it with semi-implicit time stepping.
:::

## 2. Motion planning {#ch2}

Motion planning finds a collision-free motion from a start configuration to a goal configuration. The key idea is to plan in the configuration space of [ch. 1](#ch1), where the robot is a point, rather than in the workspace, where it is a complicated body.

### The planning problem

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Free space and path]{.tag} Let $\mathcal{A}(q)$ be the set of points occupied by the robot at configuration $q$, and $\mathcal{O}$ the obstacles. The obstacle region and the free space are
$$
\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{obs}} = \{ q : \mathcal{A}(q) \cap \mathcal{O} \neq \emptyset \}, \qquad \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{free}} = \mathcal{Q} \setminus \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{obs}} .
$$

A *path* is a continuous map $\sigma : [0, 1] \to \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{free}}$ with $\sigma(0) = q_s$ and $\sigma(1) = q_g$. A planner is *complete* if it returns a path whenever one exists and reports failure otherwise.
:::

Complete planning is hard. Reif (1979) proved that the generalised “mover's problem” is PSPACE-hard, and the exact algorithms that exist are exponential in the number of degrees of freedom. Practical planners give up exact completeness: they discretise the space (resolution completeness) or sample it (probabilistic completeness).

### Search on a graph: A\*

On a grid or a roadmap, planning is a shortest-path problem on a graph with non-negative edge costs $c(u, v)$. Dijkstra's algorithm expands vertices by increasing cost-to-come $g(v)$; A\* (Hart, Nilsson and Raphael, 1968) expands them by $g(v) + h(v)$, where the heuristic $h$ estimates the cost-to-go.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — Optimality of A\*]{.tag} Suppose the heuristic is *consistent*: $h(v_{\mathrm{goal}}) = 0$ and
$$
h(u) \leq c(u, v) + h(v) \quad \text{for every edge } (u, v).
$$
Then A\* expands every vertex at most once and returns a shortest path.

::: proof
Define the reduced costs $c'(u, v) = c(u, v) - h(u) + h(v)$, which are non-negative by consistency. Along any path from $v_s$ to $v$, the reduced costs telescope:
$$
\sum c' = \sum c + h(v) - h(v_s).
$$

So A\* with costs $c$ is exactly Dijkstra's algorithm with costs $c'$: the priorities differ by the constant $h(v_s)$. Dijkstra with non-negative costs settles each vertex once, at its shortest reduced distance.

All paths from $v_s$ to the goal have their cost shifted by the same constant $-h(v_s)$, because $h(v_{\mathrm{goal}}) = 0$. Shortest paths for $c'$ are therefore shortest paths for $c$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The Euclidean distance to the goal is a consistent heuristic on any geometric graph, by the triangle inequality. Grids, however, scale as $(1/\delta)^d$ with the resolution $\delta$ and the dimension $d$: a seven-joint arm needs another idea.

### Sampling-based planning: PRM and RRT

The *probabilistic roadmap* (PRM; Kavraki, Švestka, Latombe and Overmars, 1996) samples $N$ configurations uniformly in $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{free}}$. It connects every pair closer than a radius $r$ whose straight segment is collision-free, and answers queries by graph search. Only two primitives are needed: a collision test for a configuration and one for a segment.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — Failure probability of the PRM]{.tag} In $\mathcal{Q} \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, suppose a path of length $L$ from $q_s$ to $q_g$ has *clearance* $r$: the ball of radius $r$ around each of its points is free.

Let $\mu$ denote volume and set $m = \lceil 2L / r \rceil$.

A PRM with $N$ uniform samples and connection radius $r$, with $q_s$ and $q_g$ added to the roadmap, connects them except with probability at most
$$
m \Big( 1 - \frac{\mu(B_{r/4})}{\mu(\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{free}})} \Big)^N \ \leq \ m \exp\Big( - N \frac{\mu(B_{r/4})}{\mu(\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{free}})} \Big).
$$

::: proof
Place points $y_0 = q_s, y_1, \dots, y_m = q_g$ along the path, at arc-length spacing at most $L/m \leq r/2$.

Suppose each ball $B(y_i, r/4)$ with $0 < i < m$ contains a sample $x_i$, and set $x_0 = q_s$, $x_m = q_g$.

-   Consecutive samples are close: $\|x_i - x_{i+1}\| \leq r/4 + r/2 + r/4 = r$, so the PRM tries to connect them.
-   Both endpoints lie in the ball $B(y_i, 3r/4)$, which is convex, so the whole segment does too. That ball lies in $B(y_i, r) \subset \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{free}}$: the segment is collision-free.

So failure requires that one of the $m - 1$ balls receives no sample. A given ball is missed by all $N$ independent samples with probability
$$
\big(1 - \mu(B_{r/4}) / \mu(\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{free}})\big)^N ,
$$
and the union bound concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 2.4 — How many samples?]{.tag} In the unit square with $\mu(\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{free}}) = 0.8$, take a path of length $L = 1.7$ and clearance $r = 0.1$. Then $m = 34$, and each ball of radius $0.025$ has relative volume $p = \pi (0.025)^2 / 0.8 \approx 0.00245$.

The bound is $34\, (1 - p)^N$:

-   about $0.25$ for $N = 2{,}000$;
-   about $1.6 \times 10^{-4}$ for $N = 5{,}000$.

The failure probability decays exponentially in $N$, but the rate depends on the clearance: narrow passages are the enemy of sampling.
:::

The *rapidly-exploring random tree* (RRT; LaValle, 1998; LaValle and Kuffner, 2001) grows a single tree from $q_s$. At each iteration it samples $q_{\mathrm{rand}}$ and finds the nearest tree vertex $q_{\mathrm{near}}$. It moves from $q_{\mathrm{near}}$ towards $q_{\mathrm{rand}}$ by at most a step $\eta$, and adds the new vertex if the segment is free.

Large Voronoi cells attract samples, so the tree rushes into unexplored regions. RRT is probabilistically complete but not optimal. Karaman and Frazzoli (2011) proved that, with probability one, its solution does not converge to an optimal path. Their RRT\* rewires the tree within a radius shrinking like $(\log n / n)^{1/d}$, and is asymptotically optimal.

### From paths to trajectories

A sampled path zigzags. *Shortcutting* replaces a sub-path by a straight segment whenever that segment is free. Then a *time scaling* $s(t)$ turns the geometric path $\sigma(s)$ into a trajectory $\sigma(s(t))$ that respects velocity and torque limits.

For a rest-to-rest motion, the cubic scaling $s(t) = 3 (t/T)^2 - 2 (t/T)^3$ has peak speed $1.5 / T$ at mid-course. On a path of length $L$ with a speed limit $v_{\max}$, it needs
$$
T \geq 1.5\, L / v_{\max}.
$$

Time-optimal scaling under torque limits is a classical problem (Bobrow, Dubowsky and Gibson, 1985). Planning directly with dynamics — *kinodynamic* planning — merges with the optimal control of [ch. 4](#ch4). Artificial potential fields (Khatib, 1986) are a reactive alternative, fast but trapped by local minima.

The code below runs an RRT in a square with three discs. The straight line is blocked, and the gaps between the discs are narrower than the step, so the tree must go around. Shortcutting then shortens the path.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
obstacles = [((0.5, 0.5), 0.2), ((0.25, 0.75), 0.15), ((0.75, 0.25), 0.15)]  # (centre, radius)
start, goal = np.array([0.05, 0.05]), np.array([0.95, 0.95])

def free(p):
    return all(np.linalg.norm(p - np.array(c)) > r for c, r in obstacles)

def segment_free(a, b, step=0.005):
    n = max(2, int(np.linalg.norm(b - a) / step) + 1)
    return all(free(a + t * (b - a)) for t in np.linspace(0, 1, n))

def rrt(eta=0.05, goal_bias=0.05, max_iter=5000):
    nodes, parent = [start], [-1]
    for it in range(max_iter):
        x_rand = goal if rng.random() < goal_bias else rng.random(2)
        i_near = int(np.argmin([np.linalg.norm(x_rand - v) for v in nodes]))
        d = x_rand - nodes[i_near]
        x_new = nodes[i_near] + d * min(1.0, eta / (np.linalg.norm(d) + 1e-12))
        if not segment_free(nodes[i_near], x_new):
            continue
        nodes.append(x_new); parent.append(i_near)
        if np.linalg.norm(x_new - goal) < eta and segment_free(x_new, goal):
            nodes.append(goal); parent.append(len(nodes) - 2)
            path, i = [], len(nodes) - 1
            while i >= 0:
                path.append(nodes[i]); i = parent[i]
            return path[::-1], it + 1, len(nodes)
    return None, max_iter, len(nodes)

def shortcut(path):
    """Greedy shortcutting: jump to the farthest vertex visible from the current one."""
    out, i = [path[0]], 0
    while i < len(path) - 1:
        j = len(path) - 1
        while j > i + 1 and not segment_free(path[i], path[j]):
            j -= 1
        out.append(path[j]); i = j
    return out

length = lambda p: sum(np.linalg.norm(b - a) for a, b in zip(p, p[1:]))
path, iters, n_nodes = rrt()
short = shortcut(path)
print(f"RRT: {iters} iterations, {n_nodes} nodes, path of {len(path)} vertices, length {length(path):.3f}")
print(f"after shortcutting: {len(short)} vertices, length {length(short):.3f}")
print(f"straight line {np.linalg.norm(goal - start):.3f} (blocked by the central disc: {not segment_free(start, goal)})")
```

With this seed, the tree reaches the goal after 500 iterations with 206 vertices. Its path has length 2.22; shortcutting reduces it to 1.71 with a single intermediate vertex, against 1.27 for the blocked straight line.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   Plan in configuration space, where the robot is a point and obstacles are the region $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{obs}}$.
-   A\* with a consistent heuristic is Dijkstra on reduced costs, hence optimal.
-   Sampling-based planners need only collision tests; the PRM fails with a probability that decays exponentially in the number of samples, at a rate set by the clearance.
-   RRT explores fast but is not optimal; RRT\* is asymptotically optimal.
-   Shortcutting and time scaling turn a path into an executable trajectory.
:::

## 3. Inverse problems for robot control {#ch3}

A task is specified for the end effector — reach this point, follow this line, push with this force — but the robot is commanded through its joints. Each level of control is therefore an inverse problem: positions (inverse geometry), velocities (differential kinematics), accelerations and torques (inverse dynamics).

### Inverse geometry

::: ex
[Example 3.1 — Closed-form inverse kinematics of the two-link arm]{.tag} For a target $(x, y)$ of Example 1.4, the law of cosines gives
$$
\cos q_2 = \frac{x^2 + y^2 - l_1^2 - l_2^2}{2 l_1 l_2},
\qquad
q_1 = \operatorname{atan2}(y, x) - \operatorname{atan2}(l_2 \sin q_2, \ l_1 + l_2 \cos q_2).
$$

-   For the target $(0.978, 1.187)$, $\cos q_2 = 0.4536$, so $q_2 = \pm 1.1$: two solutions, elbow up and elbow down.
-   When $|\cos q_2| > 1$ the target is out of reach, and when $|\cos q_2| = 1$ the two solutions merge at a singularity.
:::

Closed forms exist only for special geometries. In general, inverse geometry is posed as nonlinear least squares, with $e(q) = x^\star - f(q)$:
$$
\min_q \ \tfrac12 \| x^\star - f(q) \|^2 .
$$

Linearising $f$ at the current iterate and solving the damped problem of Proposition 0.3 gives the Levenberg–Marquardt step
$$
\Delta q = J^\top (J J^\top + \lambda I)^{-1} e .
$$
The damping is decreased after a successful step and increased after a failed one.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — The damped step is a descent direction]{.tag} If $J^\top e \neq 0$ and $\lambda > 0$, the Levenberg–Marquardt step decreases the objective for a small enough step length.

::: proof
By Proposition 0.3, $\Delta q = (J^\top J + \lambda I)^{-1} J^\top e$. The gradient of the objective is $-J^\top e$, and
$$
\langle -J^\top e, \Delta q \rangle = -(J^\top e)^\top (J^\top J + \lambda I)^{-1} (J^\top e) < 0,
$$
because the matrix in the middle is positive definite. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A large $\lambda$ gives a short gradient step; a small one gives the fast Gauss–Newton step. Damped least squares in inverse kinematics was introduced by Wampler (1986) and by Nakamura and Hanafusa (1986).

### Differential kinematics and redundancy

When the robot has more joints than the task has dimensions ($n > m$), the task does not determine the joint velocities.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.3 — All solutions and the null-space projector]{.tag} Let $J \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ have full row rank. The solutions of $J \dot q = v$ are exactly
$$
\dot q = J^+ v + (I - J^+ J)\, z, \qquad z \in \mathbb{R}^n .
$$
$J^+ v$ is the solution of smallest norm, and $P = I - J^+ J$ is the orthogonal projector onto $\ker J$.

::: proof
With $J^+ = J^\top (J J^\top)^{-1}$, one has $J J^+ = I$, so $J^+ v$ is a solution and $J P = J - J = 0$.

$P$ is symmetric, and $P^2 = P$ because $J^+ J J^+ = J^+$.

Its range is $\ker J$: it lies in $\ker J$ since $J P = 0$, and $P z = z$ whenever $J z = 0$.

Any solution differs from $J^+ v$ by an element of $\ker J$, that is by some $P z$.

Finally $J^+ v$ lies in the range of $J^\top$, orthogonal to $\ker J$, so adding $P z$ can only increase the norm. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The free vector $z$ serves a secondary objective: avoid joint limits, stay away from singularities, keep a posture. The *task-priority* scheme (Nakamura, Hanafusa and Yoshikawa, 1987; Siciliano and Slotine, 1991) projects a second task $J_2 \dot q = v_2$ into the null space of the first:
$$
\dot q = J_1^+ v_1 + (J_2 P_1)^+ \big( v_2 - J_2 J_1^+ v_1 \big).
$$

Integrating velocities lets the error drift. Closed-loop inverse kinematics adds a feedback term on the task error.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.4 — Closed-loop inverse kinematics]{.tag} Let $x^\star(t)$ be a desired trajectory, $e = x^\star - f(q)$, and $k > 0$. If $J(q)$ keeps full row rank along the motion, the control
$$
\dot q = J^+ (\dot x^\star + k\, e)
$$
gives $\dot e = -k e$, hence $e(t) = e^{-kt} e(0)$.

::: proof
Since $J J^+ = I$,
$$
\dot e = \dot x^\star - J \dot q = \dot x^\star - J J^+ (\dot x^\star + k e) = -k e .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The code below solves inverse geometry for a three-link planar arm, first for a reachable target, then for an unreachable one. It then solves the reachable task again with a null-space term $z = -q$ that pulls the joints towards zero.

```python
import numpy as np

L = np.array([1.0, 0.8, 0.5])            # three-link planar arm, reach 2.3 m

def fk(q):
    a = np.cumsum(q)                      # absolute link angles
    return np.array([L @ np.cos(a), L @ np.sin(a)])

def jac(q):
    a = np.cumsum(q)
    return np.array([[-L[j:] @ np.sin(a[j:]) for j in range(3)],
                     [ L[j:] @ np.cos(a[j:]) for j in range(3)]])

def ik_lm(x_star, q0, lam=1e-2, tol=1e-12, max_iter=200):
    """Levenberg-Marquardt on 1/2 |x* - fk(q)|^2, damping adapted to progress."""
    q = q0.copy()
    for k in range(max_iter):
        e = x_star - fk(q)
        if e @ e < tol:
            break
        J = jac(q)
        q_try = q + J.T @ np.linalg.solve(J @ J.T + lam * np.eye(2), e)
        if np.linalg.norm(x_star - fk(q_try)) < np.linalg.norm(e):
            q, lam = q_try, lam / 2          # success: trust the Gauss-Newton model more
        else:
            lam = lam * 10                   # failure: shorter, gradient-like step
    return q, k

q0, x_star = np.array([0.3, 0.3, 0.3]), np.array([1.2, 1.0])
q, k = ik_lm(x_star, q0)
print(f"reachable target: {k} iterations, q = {np.round(q, 4)}, error {np.linalg.norm(x_star - fk(q)):.1e}")
q_lm = q
far = np.array([3.0, 0.0])
q, k = ik_lm(far, q0)
print(f"unreachable target: q = {np.round(q, 4) + 0.0}, residual {np.linalg.norm(far - fk(q)):.4f} (= 3.0 - 2.3)")

# Redundancy: same target, secondary task "stay close to q = 0" projected in the null space
q = q0.copy()
for _ in range(400):
    J = jac(q); Jp = np.linalg.pinv(J)
    dq = Jp @ (2.0 * (x_star - fk(q))) + (np.eye(3) - Jp @ J) @ (-q)
    q = q + 0.05 * dq
print(f"with a null-space task: q = {np.round(q, 4)}, |q| = {np.linalg.norm(q):.4f} "
      f"(Levenberg-Marquardt: {np.linalg.norm(q_lm):.4f}), error {np.linalg.norm(x_star - fk(q)):.1e}")
```

The reachable target is met in 6 iterations. For the unreachable one, the method converges to the stretched arm pointing at the target, at the best possible distance $0.7$ m, instead of diverging. The null-space term reaches the same target with a smaller joint norm (1.513 against 1.530): the secondary task acts without disturbing the primary one.

### Inverse dynamics and torque control

Kinematic control assumes that the joints follow their commands. Fast or heavy robots need torque control, which inverts the dynamics of Theorem 1.7. Write $h(q, \dot q) = C(q, \dot q) \dot q + g(q)$.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.5 — Computed torque]{.tag} Let $q_d(t)$ be a twice differentiable reference, $e = q_d - q$, and $K_p, K_d$ diagonal positive definite. The control
$$
\tau = M(q) \big( \ddot q_d + K_d \dot e + K_p e \big) + h(q, \dot q)
$$
gives the linear error dynamics $\ddot e + K_d \dot e + K_p e = 0$, which converge exponentially to zero.

::: proof
Substituting $\tau$ into $M \ddot q + h = \tau$ and cancelling $h$ gives $M (\ddot q_d - \ddot q + K_d \dot e + K_p e) = 0$. Since $M \succ 0$, the bracket vanishes; it is the stated equation, whose characteristic roots have negative real parts. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Computed torque needs an exact model. A much simpler law needs only gravity.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.6 — PD plus gravity compensation (Takegaki and Arimoto, 1981)]{.tag} For a constant target $q_d$ and $K_p, K_d \succ 0$, the control
$$
\tau = K_p (q_d - q) - K_d \dot q + g(q)
$$
makes $(q, \dot q) = (q_d, 0)$ globally asymptotically stable.

::: proof
Take $V = \tfrac12 \dot q^\top M \dot q + \tfrac12 e^\top K_p e$ with $e = q_d - q$, so that $\dot e = -\dot q$. Then
$$
\dot V = \dot q^\top M \ddot q + \tfrac12 \dot q^\top \dot M \dot q - \dot q^\top K_p e .
$$

Substitute $M \ddot q = \tau - C \dot q - g = K_p e - K_d \dot q - C \dot q$. By the skew-symmetry of Proposition 1.8,
$$
\dot V = -\dot q^\top K_d \dot q \leq 0 .
$$

LaSalle's invariance principle applies, $V$ being radially unbounded. On the set where $\dot V = 0$ we have $\dot q \equiv 0$, hence $\ddot q = 0$ and $0 = K_p e$, so $e = 0$. The largest invariant set is the target. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Task-space inverse dynamics as a quadratic program

A humanoid must track several tasks while respecting its dynamics, its contacts and its torque limits. Modern controllers solve, at every control period (typically 1 ms), a quadratic program in $(\ddot q, \tau, \lambda)$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\ddot q, \tau, \lambda} \ & \| J_t \ddot q + \dot J_t \dot q - \ddot x_t^\star \|^2 + \epsilon \|\ddot q\|^2 \\
\text{s.t.} \ & M \ddot q + h = S^\top \tau + J_c^\top \lambda, \quad J_c \ddot q + \dot J_c \dot q = 0, \\
& \lambda \in \text{linearised friction cones}, \quad \tau_{\min} \leq \tau \leq \tau_{\max} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $S$ selects the actuated joints (the floating base has no motor), and the second equality keeps the contact points fixed. The reference $\ddot x_t^\star$ comes from a PD law on the task, as in Proposition 3.5.

With equality constraints only, Proposition 0.4 solves the problem with one KKT system. With strict priorities between tasks, a hierarchy of such programs is solved, efficiently, by the hierarchical quadratic programming of Escande, Mansard and Wieber (2014).

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   Inverse geometry is nonlinear least squares; Levenberg–Marquardt steps are descent directions and stay bounded near singularities.
-   Redundancy is handled by the null-space projector $I - J^+ J$; priorities stack tasks without disturbing the first.
-   Closed-loop inverse kinematics makes the task error decay exponentially.
-   Computed torque linearises the dynamics exactly; PD plus gravity is globally stable thanks to the skew-symmetry of $\dot M - 2C$.
-   Whole-body control is a quadratic program over accelerations, torques and contact forces, solved at every control period.
:::

## 4. Optimal control and trajectory optimisation {#ch4}

Inverse kinematics and computed torque track a motion that someone has designed. Optimal control designs the motion itself: among all control signals that respect the dynamics, it picks the one that minimises a cost — effort, time, distance to a goal.

### Dynamic programming

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Discrete-time optimal control problem]{.tag} Given dynamics $x_{t+1} = f(x_t, u_t)$, a running cost $\ell$ and a terminal cost $\ell_N$, find controls $u_0, \dots, u_{N-1}$ that minimise
$$
J = \sum_{t=0}^{N-1} \ell(x_t, u_t) + \ell_N(x_N)
$$
from a given initial state $x_0$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.2 — Bellman's principle]{.tag} Define the value functions backwards by $V_N = \ell_N$ and
$$
V_t(x) = \min_u \ \big[ \ell(x, u) + V_{t+1}(f(x, u)) \big].
$$
Then $V_0(x_0)$ is the optimal cost, and choosing at each time a minimiser $u_t = \pi_t(x_t)$ is optimal.

*Proof sketch.* By backward induction, $V_t(x)$ is the optimal cost-to-go from state $x$ at time $t$. The tail of an optimal trajectory must be optimal for the tail problem; otherwise replacing it would lower the total cost.
::::

The theorem returns a *feedback* law, not just a trajectory, but it requires a minimisation over $u$ for every state: tabulating $V_t$ is impossible beyond a few dimensions. One structure escapes this curse exactly.

### The linear-quadratic regulator

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.3 — Discrete-time LQR]{.tag} Let $f(x, u) = A x + B u$, $\ell(x, u) = x^\top Q x + u^\top R u$ and $\ell_N(x) = x^\top Q_N x$, with $Q, Q_N \succeq 0$ and $R \succ 0$.

Then $V_t(x) = x^\top P_t x$, the optimal control is the linear feedback $u_t = -K_t x_t$, and with $P_N = Q_N$:
$$
K_t = (R + B^\top P_{t+1} B)^{-1} B^\top P_{t+1} A,
\qquad
P_t = Q + A^\top P_{t+1} (A - B K_t).
$$

::: proof
By induction, assume $V_{t+1}(x) = x^\top P_{t+1} x$ with $P_{t+1} \succeq 0$. The Bellman minimand
$$
x^\top Q x + u^\top R u + (A x + B u)^\top P_{t+1} (A x + B u)
$$
is strictly convex in $u$, since $R + B^\top P_{t+1} B \succ 0$.

Setting its gradient in $u$ to zero gives $u = -K_t x$. Substituting back, the value is $x^\top P_t x$ with $P_t$ as stated, and $P_t \succeq 0$ as a minimum of non-negative quantities. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Over a long horizon, $P_t$ converges to the solution of the *discrete algebraic Riccati equation* when $(A, B)$ is stabilisable and $(A, Q^{1/2})$ detectable. The stationary gain then stabilises the system.

::: ex
[Example 4.4 — A scalar LQR]{.tag} Take $a = 1$, $b = 0.5$, $q = 1$, $r = 0.1$. The stationary Riccati equation $p = q + a^2 p - (a b p)^2 / (r + b^2 p)$ reduces to
$$
p^2 - p - 0.4 = 0, \qquad p = \frac{1 + \sqrt{2.6}}{2} \approx 1.306 .
$$

-   The gain is $K = a b p / (r + b^2 p) \approx 1.531$.
-   The closed loop $x_{t+1} = (a - b K) x_t$ has pole $0.234$: the error shrinks by a factor four at each step.

[Chapter 6](#ch6) will rediscover this gain by trial and error.
:::

### Pontryagin's maximum principle

In continuous time, with $\dot x = f(x, u)$ and cost $\int_0^T \ell(x, u)\, dt + \ell_T(x(T))$, the necessary conditions take the form of a two-point boundary value problem. Define the Hamiltonian
$$
H(x, u, p) = \ell(x, u) + p^\top f(x, u).
$$

::: thm
[Theorem 4.5 — Maximum principle (minimum form)]{.tag} If $u^\star$ is optimal, with trajectory $x^\star$, there is a costate $p(t)$ such that
$$
\dot x^\star = \frac{\partial H}{\partial p}, \qquad \dot p = -\frac{\partial H}{\partial x},
$$
and for almost every $t$, $u^\star(t)$ minimises $H(x^\star(t), \cdot, p(t))$ over the admissible controls. Boundary conditions complete the system: a fixed final state, or the transversality condition $p(T) = \nabla \ell_T(x^\star(T))$ when it is free.

The proof, by needle variations, is out of scope; see chapter 4 of Liberzon (2011).
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.6 — Minimum-energy transfer of a double integrator]{.tag} Move a unit mass from rest at 0 to rest at 1 in time 1, with $\ddot x = u$ and cost $\int_0^1 u^2 dt$.

1.  With state $(x, v)$, the Hamiltonian is $u^2 + p_1 v + p_2 u$.
2.  The costate equations are $\dot p_1 = 0$ and $\dot p_2 = -p_1$, so $p_2$ is affine in $t$.
3.  Minimising $H$ gives $u = -p_2 / 2$, so $u(t) = a + b t$.
4.  The four boundary conditions give $a = 6$ and $b = -12$.

The optimal control and its cost are
$$
u(t) = 6 - 12 t, \qquad \int_0^1 u^2\, dt = 12 .
$$
:::

### Direct methods and differential dynamic programming

Robots have nonlinear dynamics, constraints and dozens of states. Practical solvers discretise first and optimise afterwards:

-   **single shooting** optimises the controls only, the states being obtained by simulation; simple, but badly conditioned for unstable systems;
-   **multiple shooting** and **collocation** also treat the states as variables, linked by the dynamics as equality constraints. The resulting large, sparse nonlinear program is solved by sequential quadratic programming or interior points.

*Differential dynamic programming* (DDP; Mayne, 1966) applies Bellman's principle locally around a nominal trajectory $(\bar x_t, \bar u_t)$. Its iterative-LQR variant (iLQR; Li and Todorov, 2004) linearises the dynamics, $\delta x_{t+1} \approx A_t \delta x_t + B_t \delta u_t$, and expands the cost to second order. It then solves the resulting LQ problem by the backward recursion
$$
Q_u = \ell_u + B_t^\top V'_x, \quad Q_{uu} = \ell_{uu} + B_t^\top V'_{xx} B_t, \quad Q_{ux} = \ell_{ux} + B_t^\top V'_{xx} A_t,
$$
where $V'$ is the quadratic model of the value at time $t + 1$. The step is $\delta u_t = k_t + K_t \delta x_t$, with $k_t = -Q_{uu}^{-1} Q_u$ and $K_t = -Q_{uu}^{-1} Q_{ux}$.

A forward simulation with a line search on $k_t$ produces the next nominal trajectory. DDP also keeps the second derivatives of $f$, which iLQR drops. The Crocoddyl library (Mastalli and coauthors, 2020) implements DDP for multi-contact robots on top of Pinocchio.

The code computes the LQR gain of a double integrator by the Riccati recursion and checks it against SciPy. It then swings up a damped pendulum with iLQR, from rest hanging down to the upright position in 5 s.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import solve_discrete_are

# (a) LQR for the double integrator, state (position, velocity), period dt = 0.1 s
dt = 0.1
A = np.array([[1.0, dt], [0.0, 1.0]]); B = np.array([[dt**2 / 2], [dt]])
Q, R = np.diag([1.0, 0.1]), np.array([[0.01]])
P = Q.copy()
for _ in range(500):                                   # Riccati recursion, backwards in time
    K = np.linalg.solve(R + B.T @ P @ B, B.T @ P @ A)
    P = Q + A.T @ P @ (A - B @ K)
P_are = solve_discrete_are(A, B, Q, R)
print("K from the recursion:", np.round(K, 4), "| max |P - P_are| =", f"{np.abs(P - P_are).max():.1e}")
print("closed-loop eigenvalue moduli:", np.round(np.abs(np.linalg.eigvals(A - B @ K)), 4))

# (b) iLQR swing-up of a damped pendulum (theta = 0 hanging down, target theta = pi)
m, l, g, b, h, N = 1.0, 1.0, 9.81, 0.1, 0.05, 100      # 100 steps of 50 ms
x_goal, r, w_T = np.array([np.pi, 0.0]), 1e-2, 1e3

def f(x, u):                                           # explicit Euler discretisation
    return np.array([x[0] + h * x[1], x[1] + h * (-g / l * np.sin(x[0]) - b * x[1] + u / (m * l**2))])

def f_x(x):
    return np.array([[1.0, h], [-h * g / l * np.cos(x[0]), 1.0 - h * b]])

f_u = np.array([0.0, h / (m * l**2)])

def cost(X, U):
    e = X[-1] - x_goal
    return r * U @ U + w_T * e @ e

U = np.zeros(N)
X = np.zeros((N + 1, 2))
for t in range(N):
    X[t + 1] = f(X[t], U[t])
J = cost(X, U)
for it in range(200):
    Vx, Vxx = 2 * w_T * (X[-1] - x_goal), 2 * w_T * np.eye(2)    # backward pass
    k_ff, K_fb = np.zeros(N), np.zeros((N, 2))
    for t in reversed(range(N)):
        At = f_x(X[t])
        Qx, Qu = At.T @ Vx, 2 * r * U[t] + f_u @ Vx
        Qxx, Quu, Qux = At.T @ Vxx @ At, 2 * r + f_u @ Vxx @ f_u, f_u @ Vxx @ At
        k_ff[t], K_fb[t] = -Qu / Quu, -Qux / Quu
        Vx = Qx + Qux * k_ff[t]                                   # value of the optimal step
        Vxx = Qxx - np.outer(Qux, Qux) / Quu
    for alpha in [1.0, 0.5, 0.25, 0.1, 0.03, 0.01]:               # forward pass + line search
        Xn, Un = np.zeros_like(X), np.zeros(N)
        Xn[0] = X[0]
        for t in range(N):
            Un[t] = U[t] + alpha * k_ff[t] + K_fb[t] @ (Xn[t] - X[t])
            Xn[t + 1] = f(Xn[t], Un[t])
        if cost(Xn, Un) < J:
            break
    if J - cost(Xn, Un) < 1e-9 * J:
        break
    X, U, J = Xn, Un, cost(Xn, Un)
print(f"iLQR: {it} iterations, cost {J:.3f}, final state {np.round(X[-1], 4)}, max |u| = {np.abs(U).max():.2f} N m")
```

The recursion matches SciPy to $10^{-13}$ and both closed-loop poles have modulus 0.76. iLQR converges in 46 iterations to a final angle of 3.1405 rad with a peak torque of 2.66 N m. That is about a quarter of the torque $m g l = 9.81$ N m needed to hold the pendulum horizontal, so the optimiser has discovered that it must pump energy by swinging.

### Model predictive control

An open-loop trajectory fails at the first disturbance. *Model predictive control* (MPC) closes the loop by re-optimising.

::: def
[Definition 4.7 — Receding horizon]{.tag} At each control period, measure the state $x$, solve the optimal control problem of horizon $N$ from $x$, apply only the first control $u_0^\star(x)$, and repeat at the next period.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.8 — Stability with a terminal cost (sketch)]{.tag} Suppose the terminal cost $V_f$ admits a local feedback $\kappa_f$ such that, on a terminal set $\mathbb{X}_f$ that $\kappa_f$ keeps invariant,
$$
V_f\big(f(x, \kappa_f(x))\big) - V_f(x) \leq -\ell\big(x, \kappa_f(x)\big),
$$
and suppose the MPC problem includes the constraint $x_N \in \mathbb{X}_f$. Then the optimal value $V_N^\star$ decreases along the closed loop by at least $\ell(x, u_0^\star)$, and is a Lyapunov function.

::: proof
At the next state $x^+$, the shifted sequence $u_1^\star, \dots, u_{N-1}^\star$ followed by $\kappa_f(x_N^\star)$ is feasible. Its cost is $V_N^\star(x) - \ell(x, u_0^\star)$, plus the terminal difference of the assumption, which is non-positive. The optimum at $x^+$ is no larger. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This argument, surveyed by Mayne, Rawlings, Rao and Scokaert (2000), underlies the walking controllers of [ch. 7](#ch7), which re-solve a small MPC problem at every control period.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   Bellman's principle gives optimal feedback by backward recursion; it is tractable exactly in the linear-quadratic case.
-   The LQR gain comes from a Riccati recursion; the stationary gain stabilises the system.
-   Pontryagin's principle gives necessary conditions as a boundary-value problem with a costate.
-   Direct methods (shooting, collocation) and DDP/iLQR solve nonlinear trajectory optimisation; iLQR is a sequence of local LQR problems.
-   MPC re-optimises at every period; a terminal cost and set make its value a Lyapunov function.
:::

## 5. Perception and estimation {#ch5}

A controller needs the state of the robot — its pose, its velocity, the position of the objects around it — but sensors give only noisy, partial measurements. Estimation fuses a model of the motion with these measurements; perception extracts geometric information from cameras and range sensors.

### Sensors and the filtering problem

Robots measure themselves with joint encoders, force sensors and inertial measurement units (gyroscopes and accelerometers). They measure the world with cameras, depth cameras and LiDAR. Both kinds of measurement are summarised by a state-space model:
$$
x_{k+1} = f(x_k, u_k) + w_k, \qquad y_k = h(x_k) + v_k ,
$$
with process noise $w_k$ and measurement noise $v_k$.

The *Bayes filter* propagates the distribution of $x_k$ given $y_{0:k}$ in two steps. The prediction integrates the motion model against the previous posterior; the update multiplies by the likelihood $p(y_{k+1} \mid x_{k+1})$ and renormalises. Two cases are tractable: linear-Gaussian models (Kalman filter) and low dimensions, or many particles (particle filters, see [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html)).

### The Kalman filter

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.1 — Kalman filter (Kalman, 1960)]{.tag} Let $f(x, u) = F x + G u$ and $h(x) = H x$, with independent Gaussian noises of covariances $Q$ and $R$ and a Gaussian prior.

The posterior of $x_k$ given $y_{0:k}$ is Gaussian, $\mathcal{N}(m_k, P_k)$, computed by the following recursion.

-   **Predict**: $m^- = F m_{k-1} + G u_{k-1}$ and $P^- = F P_{k-1} F^\top + Q$.
-   **Update**: with the innovation covariance $S = H P^- H^\top + R$ and the gain $K = P^- H^\top S^{-1}$,
$$
m_k = m^- + K (y_k - H m^-), \qquad P_k = (I - K H) P^- .
$$

::: proof
By induction, suppose the posterior at time $k - 1$ is $\mathcal{N}(m_{k-1}, P_{k-1})$. The state $x_k$ is an affine function of $x_{k-1}$ plus independent Gaussian noise: given $y_{0:k-1}$, it is Gaussian with the predicted moments.

The pair $(x_k, y_k)$ is then jointly Gaussian given $y_{0:k-1}$, with $\mathrm{Cov}(x_k, y_k) = P^- H^\top$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(y_k) = S$. Gaussian conditioning (Proposition 0.9) gives exactly the update formulas. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 5.2 — One update by hand]{.tag} A scalar position has prior $\mathcal{N}(0, 4)$, and a sensor of noise variance $1$ returns $y = 2$.

-   The gain is $K = 4 / (4 + 1) = 0.8$.
-   The posterior mean is $0 + 0.8 \times 2 = 1.6$, and the posterior variance $(1 - 0.8) \times 4 = 0.8$.

The estimate moves most of the way towards the precise sensor, and its variance is smaller than both the prior and the sensor variances.
:::

The Riccati recursion of the covariance is the time-reversed twin of the LQR recursion of [ch. 4](#ch4): estimation and control are dual problems, as Kalman already noted.

### Nonlinear models: the EKF and observability

The *extended Kalman filter* (EKF) applies the same recursion to the linearisations $F_k = \partial f / \partial x$ and $H_k = \partial h / \partial x$ at the current estimate. It is the workhorse of robot navigation, but it has no optimality guarantee. Linearising at a wrong estimate can make it inconsistent, that is, overconfident.

Before filtering, one should ask whether the measurements determine the state at all.

::: prop
[Proposition 5.3 — Observability rank condition]{.tag} The linear system $(F, H)$ with state dimension $n$ is observable — the initial state is determined by noise-free outputs — if and only if the matrix stacking $H, HF, \dots, HF^{n-1}$ has rank $n$.

*Example.* For the constant-velocity model with position measurements, $H = (1, 0)$ and $HF = (1, \Delta t)$: rank 2, so the velocity is observable although never measured. With velocity measurements only, the rank is 1 and the position is not observable.
:::

### Estimation on Lie groups: invariant errors

Orientation lives in $SO(3)$, not in a vector space, and the EKF's additive error $R - \hat R$ is not a rotation. Bonnabel, Martin and Rouchon (2008) proposed instead errors defined with the group operation. Their behaviour can be remarkable.

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.4 — An autonomous error for attitude]{.tag} Let the true attitude obey $\dot R = R [\omega]_\times$, where $\omega$ is measured by a perfect gyroscope, and propagate the estimate with the same equation, $\dot{\hat R} = \hat R [\omega]_\times$. Then the invariant error $\eta = R \hat R^\top$ is constant, whatever the motion $\omega(t)$.

::: proof
Since $[\omega]_\times^\top = -[\omega]_\times$,
$$
\dot \eta = R [\omega]_\times \hat R^\top + R [\omega]_\times^\top \hat R^\top = 0 .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The additive error, by contrast, rotates with $\omega(t)$, and a linearisation of it depends on the trajectory. Barrau and Bonnabel (2017) generalised the observation to *group-affine* systems, a class that includes inertial navigation. For these systems, the invariant error obeys an equation that does not depend on the estimate, and its logarithm obeys an exactly linear equation.

The resulting *invariant EKF* inherits convergence properties of the linear Kalman filter that the standard EKF lacks. Hartley and coauthors (2020) built a contact-aided invariant EKF for legged robots on this basis.

### Batch estimation, SLAM and registration

Filtering processes measurements once. *Batch* estimation computes the maximum a posteriori trajectory given all measurements, as a nonlinear least-squares problem:
$$
\min_{x_{0:K}} \ \sum_k \| x_{k+1} - f(x_k, u_k) \|^2_{Q^{-1}} + \sum_k \| y_k - h(x_k) \|^2_{R^{-1}} .
$$

Gauss–Newton solves it with sparse linear algebra, because each term involves one or two states. In the linear-Gaussian case, the solution coincides with the Kalman smoother. When the landmarks of a map join the unknowns, the problem becomes *simultaneous localisation and mapping* (SLAM). Factor graphs (Dellaert and Kaess, 2017) represent the sparsity; Barfoot's textbook develops the whole approach.

Cameras enter through the pinhole model. A point $(X, Y, Z)$ in the camera frame projects to the pixel $(f X / Z + c_x, \ f Y / Z + c_y)$, and minimising reprojection errors is *bundle adjustment*; see [3D Computer Vision](../s1-3d-computer-vision/index.html). Depth sensors give 3D points directly, and the basic problem becomes aligning two point clouds.

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.5 — Rigid registration (Kabsch–Umeyama)]{.tag} Given pairs $(p_i, q_i)$, $i = 1, \dots, n$, with centroids $\bar p, \bar q$, let
$$
W = \sum_i (q_i - \bar q)(p_i - \bar p)^\top = U S V^\top \quad \text{(SVD)}.
$$
The minimiser of $\sum_i \|q_i - R p_i - t\|^2$ over $R \in SO(3)$ and $t \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is
$$
R^\star = U\, \mathrm{diag}\big(1, 1, \det(U V^\top)\big)\, V^\top, \qquad t^\star = \bar q - R^\star \bar p .
$$

::: proof
For fixed $R$, the optimal $t$ is the least-squares fit of the residual means, $t = \bar q - R \bar p$. With centred points $\tilde p_i, \tilde q_i$, the cost becomes a constant minus $2 \sum_i \tilde q_i^\top R \tilde p_i$, and this sum equals $\mathrm{tr}(R^\top W)$.

Write $Z = U^\top R V$, which is orthogonal. Since $|Z_{ii}| \leq 1$,
$$
\mathrm{tr}(R^\top W) = \mathrm{tr}(Z^\top S) = \sum_i s_i Z_{ii} \leq \sum_i s_i .
$$
Equality holds at $Z = I$, that is $R = U V^\top$, which is a rotation when $\det(U V^\top) = 1$.

Otherwise the constraint $\det R = 1$ forces $\det Z = -1$. The best choice flips the sign of the smallest singular direction, $Z = \mathrm{diag}(1, 1, -1)$; see Umeyama (1991) for the details. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

When correspondences are unknown, the *iterative closest point* algorithm (Besl and McKay, 1992) alternates nearest-neighbour matching and Theorem 5.5. Each step decreases the cost, so ICP converges, but only to a local minimum: it needs a good initial guess.

The code runs a Kalman filter on a constant-velocity target observed in position only, then registers two noisy point clouds.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial.transform import Rotation

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
# (a) Kalman filter: constant-velocity target, only the position is measured
dt, n, sa, sr = 0.1, 200, 0.5, 1.0          # period, steps, acceleration std, measurement std
F, H = np.array([[1.0, dt], [0.0, 1.0]]), np.array([[1.0, 0.0]])
Qn = sa**2 * np.array([[dt**4 / 4, dt**3 / 2], [dt**3 / 2, dt**2]])
Rn = np.array([[sr**2]])
x, xs, ys = np.array([0.0, 1.0]), [], []
for _ in range(n):
    x = F @ x + rng.multivariate_normal(np.zeros(2), Qn)
    xs.append(x); ys.append(H @ x + sr * rng.standard_normal(1))
xs, ys = np.array(xs), np.array(ys)

m, P, est = np.zeros(2), 10.0 * np.eye(2), []
for y in ys:
    m, P = F @ m, F @ P @ F.T + Qn                        # predict
    S = H @ P @ H.T + Rn
    K = P @ H.T @ np.linalg.inv(S)                        # Kalman gain
    m, P = m + K @ (y - H @ m), (np.eye(2) - K @ H) @ P   # update
    est.append(m)
est = np.array(est)
rmse = lambda u, v: np.sqrt(np.mean((u - v) ** 2))
print(f"position RMSE: raw measurements {rmse(ys[:, 0], xs[:, 0]):.3f}, Kalman {rmse(est[:, 0], xs[:, 0]):.3f}")
print(f"velocity RMSE (never measured): {rmse(est[:, 1], xs[:, 1]):.3f}; final gain K = {np.round(K.ravel(), 3)}")

# (b) Registration of two point sets with known correspondences (Theorem 5.5)
R_true = Rotation.from_rotvec([0.2, -0.4, 0.9]).as_matrix()
t_true = np.array([0.5, -1.0, 2.0])
p = rng.standard_normal((100, 3))
q = p @ R_true.T + t_true + 0.01 * rng.standard_normal((100, 3))
pc, qc = p.mean(0), q.mean(0)
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd((q - qc).T @ (p - pc))           # W = sum (q_i - qc)(p_i - pc)^T
D = np.diag([1.0, 1.0, np.sign(np.linalg.det(U @ Vt))])
R_hat = U @ D @ Vt
t_hat = qc - R_hat @ pc
angle = np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip((np.trace(R_hat.T @ R_true) - 1) / 2, -1, 1)))
print(f"rotation error {angle:.3f} deg, translation error {np.linalg.norm(t_hat - t_true):.4f}")
```

The filter divides the position error by almost three (0.35 against 0.98 for the raw measurements). It also estimates the velocity, which is never measured, with an error of 0.27, as Proposition 5.3 promised. The registration recovers the rotation to 0.05 degree and the translation to 2 mm.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   Estimation fuses a motion model and measurements; the Bayes filter alternates prediction and update.
-   For linear-Gaussian models, the Kalman filter is exact: it is Gaussian conditioning, step after step, and it is dual to the LQR.
-   The EKF linearises; check observability before trusting any filter.
-   Errors defined with the group operation can be independent of the trajectory: the basis of the invariant EKF.
-   Batch estimation and SLAM are sparse nonlinear least squares; rigid registration has a closed form by SVD, iterated in ICP.
:::

## 6. Reinforcement learning for robotics {#ch6}

Optimal control needs a model of the dynamics and of the cost. Reinforcement learning (RL) optimises a policy from trials instead — in simulation, most of the time. It has produced the most robust legged controllers of recent years; this chapter gives its mathematical core and the conditions under which it transfers to real robots.

### Markov decision processes and optimal control

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Markov decision process]{.tag} A Markov decision process consists of states $x$, actions $u$, a transition kernel $p(x' \mid x, u)$, a cost $c(x, u)$ and a horizon (finite, or infinite with a discount factor $\gamma \in (0, 1)$).

A stochastic policy $\pi_\theta(u \mid x)$ induces a distribution over trajectories $\tau = (x_0, u_0, x_1, \dots)$, and the objective is
$$
J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_\theta} \Big[ \sum_t \gamma^t c(x_t, u_t) \Big].
$$
:::

With a known model, this is the optimal control problem of [ch. 4](#ch4), and Bellman's recursion applies with an expectation over $x'$. RL methods differ in what they learn: value functions (Q-learning), policies (policy gradient), or both (actor–critic). The [Reinforcement Learning](../s2-reinforcement-learning/index.html) course of semester 2 develops them in depth. Here, the policy-gradient family matters most, because robot actions are continuous.

### The policy-gradient theorem

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.2 — Likelihood-ratio policy gradient (Williams, 1992)]{.tag} For a finite horizon $T$ and $G_t = \sum_{s \geq t} c(x_s, u_s)$ the cost-to-go from time $t$,
$$
\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\Big[ \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(u_t \mid x_t) \, \big( G_t - b(x_t) \big) \Big]
$$
for any baseline $b$ that depends on the state only.

::: proof
The trajectory density is
$$
p_\theta(\tau) = p(x_0) \prod_t \pi_\theta(u_t \mid x_t)\, p(x_{t+1} \mid x_t, u_t).
$$
Only the policy factors depend on $\theta$, so
$$
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\tau) = \sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(u_t \mid x_t),
$$
and the unknown dynamics disappear. Differentiating $J = \int p_\theta(\tau) C(\tau)\, d\tau$ under the integral and using $\nabla p = p \nabla \log p$ gives the formula with $C(\tau)$ in place of $G_t - b$.

*Causality*: a cost incurred before time $t$ is independent of $u_t$ given the past, and
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\nabla \log \pi_\theta(u_t \mid x_t) \mid x_t\big] = \nabla \int \pi_\theta(u \mid x_t)\, du = 0 .
$$
So past costs can be dropped, leaving $G_t$; the same identity shows that $b(x_t)$ adds zero in expectation. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The estimator only needs to sample trajectories and differentiate the log-policy: no model, no derivative of the dynamics. Its variance, however, is large; the baseline reduces it without bias.

::: ex
[Example 6.3 — A linear Gaussian policy on the scalar system of Example 4.4]{.tag} Take $u = -\theta x + \sigma \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$. Then
$$
\log \pi_\theta(u \mid x) = -\frac{(u + \theta x)^2}{2 \sigma^2} + \text{const}, \qquad \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta = -\frac{\varepsilon\, x}{\sigma} .
$$
:::

The code below runs this REINFORCE estimator, with the time-wise average of $G_t$ as baseline, on $x_{t+1} = x_t + 0.5 u_t$ with cost $x^2 + 0.1 u^2$ over 30 steps. It compares the learned gain with the LQR gain of Example 4.4.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
a, b, qc, rc, T = 1.0, 0.5, 1.0, 0.1, 30       # x' = a x + b u, cost q x^2 + r u^2, horizon T

p = qc                                          # stationary scalar Riccati equation (ch. 4)
for _ in range(1000):
    p = qc + a * a * p - (a * b * p) ** 2 / (rc + b * b * p)
K_lqr = a * b * p / (rc + b * b * p)

def rollouts(theta, sigma, n):
    """n episodes of the Gaussian policy u = -theta x + sigma eps; returns states, noises, costs."""
    x = rng.standard_normal(n)
    X, E, C = np.zeros((T, n)), np.zeros((T, n)), np.zeros((T, n))
    for t in range(T):
        eps = rng.standard_normal(n)
        u = -theta * x + sigma * eps
        X[t], E[t], C[t] = x, eps, qc * x**2 + rc * u**2
        x = a * x + b * u
    return X, E, C

theta, sigma, lr = 0.0, 0.5, 0.003
for it in range(501):
    X, E, C = rollouts(theta, sigma, 500)
    G = np.cumsum(C[::-1], axis=0)[::-1]              # cost-to-go from each time step
    G = G - G.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)             # baseline: average cost-to-go at time t
    score = -E * X / sigma                            # d/dtheta log pi(u_t | x_t)
    grad = np.mean(np.sum(score * G, axis=0))         # REINFORCE estimate of dJ/dtheta
    theta -= lr * grad
    if it % 100 == 0:
        print(f"iteration {it:3d}: theta = {theta:.3f}, average cost {C.sum(0).mean():.2f}")
print(f"LQR gain K = {K_lqr:.3f}")
```

After 500 iterations of 500 episodes each, the learned gain is 1.533, against 1.531 for the LQR. RL has rediscovered the optimal controller, but it used 250,000 episodes where the Riccati equation needed one line. That ratio is the price of ignoring the model, and the reason why robot RL is done in simulation.

### Actor–critic methods: PPO and SAC

Practical algorithms replace $G_t - b(x_t)$ by an estimate of the *advantage* $A(x_t, u_t) = Q(x_t, u_t) - V(x_t)$, given by a learned critic. Proximal policy optimisation (PPO; Schulman and coauthors, 2017) maximises a clipped surrogate objective over a batch collected with the previous policy:
$$
\mathbb{E}\Big[ \min\big( \rho_t A_t, \ \mathrm{clip}(\rho_t, 1 - \epsilon, 1 + \epsilon) A_t \big) \Big], \qquad \rho_t = \frac{\pi_\theta(u_t \mid x_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(u_t \mid x_t)},
$$
